findings.problem: The credentials table classifies the 'Controlled substance registration issued by the Board' as a 'Credential held by an individual or an entity'. A Board-issued controlled substance registration is an entity credential only. 247 CMR 11.01(1) lets the Board issue one to a pharmacy, outsourcing facility or wholesale drug business. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a) sends every other registrant, including individual practitioners, to the commissioner, and has pharmacies, wholesale druggists and outsourcing facilities register with the Board of Registration in Pharmacy.
findings.rationale: Learning objective 1 asks the candidate to say which credentials in 247 CMR 10.01 are individual and which are entity credentials, and this cell gets the controlled substance registration wrong. It suggests an individual pharmacist can hold a Board-issued controlled substance registration, which is a testable Massachusetts misconception. Fix: classify it as an entity credential held by a pharmacy, outsourcing facility or wholesale drug business, citing 247 CMR 11.01(1).

findings.problem: The section reads 'without cause' as qualifying all of 247 CMR 10.03(1)(q). decision_logic[7] tells the candidate, for a missed request, a subpoena or a records demand, to 'ask only whether the failure was without cause'. In the official text 'without cause' is attached to the first limb (cooperating with a request to appear or to provide requested information). The subpoena limb and the records limb follow a semicolon, each opens with its own 'failing', and the records limb has its own element: records 'to which the Board is legally entitled'.
findings.rationale: Applied literally, the decision rule gives the subpoena limb an excuse the text does not give it, and the word 'only' drops the legal-entitlement element of the records limb. forms_records[1] itself treats the subpoena limb as covered 'in its own right'. Severity is Low because the words of (q) are quoted correctly elsewhere and MA-Q-0264 is unaffected. Fix: state the three limbs separately, keep 'without cause' on the first, and remove 'only'.

findings.problem: The section says Massachusetts discipline 'begins with a credential rather than with a person'. The worked example then calls treating discipline as an action against a person 'the error', because 247 CMR 10.01 supposedly 'frames it as an action against a credential'. The text does not support this. 10.01 lists persons and entities (registered pharmacist, pharmacy technician, pharmacy, pharmacy department) alongside two credentials (wholesale license, controlled substance registration). 10.03(1) says the Board may impose disciplinary action 'against an individual or entity licensed or registered by the Board'.
findings.rationale: The legal conclusion taught is right: the Board may proceed against both the individual and the entity, and it need not choose between them. The section, however, credits 10.01 with a framing it does not contain and calls the regulation's own framing the error. Low. Fix: reword to say the Board may proceed against each individual and entity it licenses or registers, and that nothing in 10.01 or 10.03(1) requires an election.

results.summary: Checked against the current mass.gov compilation of 247 CMR 10.00 (Mass. Register #1546, 4/25/2025; pages effective 1/9/25). The following match the official text: every quotation of 10.01, the 10.02 conviction definition, 10.03(1)(f), (g), (h), (i), (m), (q) and (t), 10.03(2), 10.03(3) and 10.06(7). The section correctly teaches the protected-care carve-out and its two qualifiers (read with M.G.L. c. 12, s. 11I1/2 and c. 112, s. 61), the out-of-state proviso, the conclusive-evidence rule and the non-exhaustive grounds list. All six practice questions (MA-Q-0262, 0264, 0267, 0268, 0270, 0272) can be answered from the section and none is contradicted. It is not publishable as it stands, for three reasons. First (Medium), one table cell misclassifies the Board-issued controlled substance registration, which is entity-only under 247 CMR 11.01(1) and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(a); this goes against learning objective 1. Second (Low), the section extends 'without cause' across all of 10.03(1)(q), and its decision rule drops the 'legally entitled' element. Third (Low), it credits 10.01 with a 'credential, not person' framing that the text does not support. Each needs only a targeted edit.

findings.problem: In the worked example the pharmacist voluntarily surrenders her registration for 18 months under a consent agreement. The example then holds that '247 CMR 4.02(6) governs' her renewal and that she must take and pass the MPJE, and step[5] adds that the agreement's reinstatement provisions 'do not displace the renewal prerequisites'. 247 CMR 4.02(6) and (7) reach a personal registration that 'has been revoked or has been suspended'. 4.02 never mentions surrender, and 247 CMR 2.00 defines none of surrender, suspension or revocation. 10.06(6) lists 'voluntary suspension or surrender' as alternatives and requires the surrender agreement itself to include 'provisions addressing reinstatement'. 10.03(1)(j) names the Surrender Agreement as an instrument distinct from a Consent Agreement and a Final Decision and Order. Step[3] also misquotes 4.02(6) by dropping 'has been' before 'suspended'.
findings.rationale: The resolution rests on a rule the text does not contain, and the section contradicts it elsewhere. timing_deadlines[8] says the agreement's own reinstatement provisions 'govern what happens next'. comparison_tables[3].rows[6] points a surrender to the agreement's own reinstatement provisions and cites 4.02(6)/(7) only in the adjudicated-outcome column. A candidate would learn that a fixed-period surrender counts as a suspension for 4.02 purposes. Fix: either recast the facts as a voluntary suspension of 18 months, or answer the renewal question from the surrender agreement's reinstatement provisions and delete step[5]'s claim.

findings.location: orientation[2] (probation sentence: 'the one formal sanction that leaves the registrant working'); retrieval_prompts[9]; exceptions[1]
findings.problem: orientation[2] calls probation 'the one formal sanction that leaves the registrant working'. retrieval_prompts[9] keys 'Probation' as the answer to which formal sanction in 247 CMR 10.06 'permits the registrant to keep practising'. exceptions[1] calls probation 'the exception to the assumption that formal discipline stops practice'. Under 10.06(3) a reprimand is formal disciplinary action and a censure is a severe reprimand, and 10.06 attaches no suspension or restriction of practice to either.
findings.rationale: Probation is the only 10.06 sanction defined as practice under Board-imposed conditions. It is not the only formal sanction that leaves the registrant practising. As written, the orientation and the retrieval answer key teach by implication that a reprimand or censure stops practice, and a candidate could carry that into a question about the effect of a reprimand or censure. Fix: describe probation as the sanction that permits continued practice subject to Board conditions, and say that reprimand and censure do not restrict practice.

findings.problem: role_duties[2] says the Board is to 'impose probation, suspension or revocation only pursuant to a formal adjudicatory hearing or an executed consent agreement'. 10.06(5) is permissive ('may be imposed'), and 10.07 lets the Board suspend or refuse to renew a license before any hearing, pending a final hearing on the merits. M.G.L. c. 112, s. 42A likewise lets the board or board president summarily suspend a pharmacy license, and M.G.L. c. 30A, s. 13 provides for suspension without a prior hearing.
findings.rationale: The word 'only' contradicts the section's own treatment of 10.07 in orientation[3], timing_deadlines[0] and role_duties[3]. Severity is Low because summary suspension is taught correctly elsewhere. Fix: limit the statement to a final suspension or revocation, or cross-refer to 10.07.

findings.location: role_duties[0]; orientation[5] (first sentence); orientation[2] ('From the third item onward the actions are formal')
findings.problem: role_duties[0] makes it the Board's duty, once it has made its determination, to 'schedule either an investigative conference or a formal adjudicatory hearing'. But 10.04 and 10.05 are permissive, and the Board may dismiss (10.06(1)) or issue an advisory letter (10.06(2)) without holding either. orientation[5] says a matter can end without a hearing and '247 CMR 10.06(6) is how', yet dismissal and an advisory letter also end a matter without one. orientation[2] says 'From the third item onward the actions are formal', but the 10.06(8) and (9) notices impose what 10.08(1) calls non-disciplinary restrictions, as the section's own comparison_tables[1].rows[6] records.
findings.rationale: These are small overstatements of the procedure that falls within the section's declared scope. A candidate could conclude that every complaint leads to a conference or a hearing, or that every 10.06 item from (3) onward is formal discipline. Low. Fix: use permissive language, and limit 'onward' to items (3) through (5).

findings.problem: The official text of 4.02(6) reads 'has been revoked or has been suspended for between six months and two years', with no comma. The section adds a comma, giving 'revoked, or suspended for between six months and two years', which puts every revocation in 4.02(6). It also quotes 4.02(7) as reaching a registration 'revoked or suspended for more than two years', so a revocation of more than two years falls in both tiers, and the section never says which governs. decision_logic[7] and comparison_tables[4].rows[4] tell the candidate to 'measure the sanction', which does not work for an indefinite revocation. common_traps[10] and role_duties[8] state that renewal after 'suspension or revocation' requires the MPJE, contradicting exceptions[5], which says neither tier applies to a suspension of less than six months.
findings.rationale: The regulation's own drafting is ambiguous and the tiers for suspensions are taught correctly, so this is Low. The fix: quote 4.02(6) exactly; state how a revocation is placed (for example, by time since revocation, with 4.02(7) governing beyond two years); and qualify common_traps[10] and role_duties[8] for suspensions under six months.

results.summary: Every period is correct in number, unit, trigger and owner: 7 days from the Board's action under 10.07; 15 business days from the Board's or Board President's action under 10.08(3); 7 business days under 10.03(1)(y) and (z); 30 days, in writing, under 10.03(1)(aa); and the six-months-to-two-years and more-than-two-years bands in 247 CMR 4.02(6) and (7). Also correct: the 10.02 definitions of complaint, investigative conference, adjudicatory hearing and Order to Show Cause; the permissive choice of track in 10.04 and 10.05; the 10.06 classification of dismissal, advisory letter, reprimand, censure and probation; the four terms of a surrender agreement; and the non-disciplinary character and duration of 10.08 notices. All eight practice questions (MA-Q-0211, 0223, 0255, 0263, 0265, 0266, 0269, 0271) can be answered from the section and none is contradicted. Two Medium defects must be fixed before publication. First, worked_examples[3] applies 4.02(6) to a voluntary surrender, which 4.02 does not reach and which the section itself routes elsewhere to the agreement's reinstatement provisions. Second, the section repeatedly presents probation as the only formal sanction that leaves the registrant practising, which is untrue of reprimand and censure. Several Low wording issues should be fixed in the same pass: 'only' in role_duties[2]; 'immediate and serious'; 'permanently' applied to voluntary suspension; the accuracy limb credited to (z); the comma inserted into 4.02(6) and the unresolved placement of revocations; and permissive steps restated as duties.
